Prevention: Do early land tillage by end of
November, to reduce growth of the weed.
Urea/ha), as over- fertilisation favours the growth of the weed.
Plant early with the first effective rains (rains of at least 30mm cumulative rain), thus before weeds germinate.
Use certified maize seeds to avoid introduction through contamination by weed seeds in the maize grains.
Intercrop maize with legumes (beans, cowpeas) to allow complete ground cover to inflict negative shading effects on the
Avoid grazing animals in the fields as they spread weed seeds in animal dung
Monitoring: Oxgrass is an invasive weed, producing more than 50,000 small seeds/plants, and competes with maize for water and nutrients.
Viable oxgrass seeds persist in the upper soil for 2-5 years.
Look for a tufted annual grass with lots of side shoots spreading upwards up to 40cm tall.
Leaves are bright green, flat to
V-shaped or folded along the main vein, up to 8mm wide and 15cm long.
Thin flower heads have 3-8 'branches', each with two dense rows of tiny greenish flowers.
Scout fields weekly after crop emergence for the presence of weeds.
Consider direct control methods when young oxgrass plants are found in 10-25 different spots of your field during sampling.
Direct Control: Remove the weed when young by hand- pulling or hoeing.
Later, the weed removal gets harder as roots grow stronger.
Restrictions: Preventive and green direct control measures are usually enough to control the weed, so there is no need for synthetic herbicides.
